citation.title: Blame the Bot: Anthropomorphism and Anger in Customer–Chatbot Interactions

reading.source_scope_note: One observational telecom dataset and four simulated service-chat experiments concern human responses to humanlike chatbot cues in angry versus comparison scenarios. They test customer ratings and purchase intentions, not an AI’s own feelings, actual purchases, deliberate retaliation or modern LLM behavior.
access_limits: All supplied main pages and six main figures were read, including the histogram, conceptual model and plotted cell means. Main bibliography was read but cited books and original emotion theories were not independently read in full.

All 59 supplementary pages were read as extracted text, including scripts, model tables and numeric figure labels. Image-only avatars, chat screenshots, network graph, emoji examples, co-occurrence table and ROC plot were not visually available: screenshot calls produced placeholders. Extracted labels do not establish complete image inspection.

No private customer transcripts, original raw field data, experiment data, participant records or analysis code obtained. No statistical model refit, reconstructed participant data, source author contact or reproduction of marginal effects performed.
Supplementary source is summarized briefly; the main supplied PDF supports the detailed review. No full supplementary transcription is saved.

study.field_sample: Study 1 covers 1,645,098 customer text entries in 461,689 sessions from September 2016 to August 2017 in one European telecom market. Sessions are not unique people. Only 34,639 sessions, approximately 7.5%, have optional 1–5 ratings; the rating subset is selected.
study.field_operationalization: All sessions encounter the same named female-avatar chatbot. Frequency of name use is the anthropomorphic-treatment proxy, not randomly assigned appearance or a direct agency scale. Anger is the session mean of LIWC anger-word proportions. Bot recognition rate is the system’s own confidence, not independently verified comprehension or service quality.
study.field_model: The specified and tabulated main analysis is a joint binary-selection and ordered-probit model with correlated errors, despite an earlier reference to ordinal logistic regression. Excluding interaction type from the rating equation is an identifying assumption. Anger and name use are not randomized, and exchange-level dynamics can create reverse direction or common causes.
study.field_results: The main name-use × anger coefficient is −.1665, z −1.96, reported around p .05. An endogenous binary-anger robustness model also reports a formal joint Wald test, chi-square(2) 6.62, p .04. Do not describe these as merely a significant subgroup alongside a nonsignificant subgroup, or as establishing that anger preceded the encounter.
study.study_2: 201 MTurk participants minus four attention exclusions leaves 197. Random assignment crosses scenario and bundled name/avatar/first-person/quotation cues. Satisfaction averages five 1–5 items. The formal interaction is F(1,193) 5.26, p .02; angry-scenario means are 2.58 control versus 2.09 anthropomorphic. Neutral means 3.16 versus 3.44 differ nonsignificantly.
study.emotion_boundaries: Study 2’s scenario pretest produces anticipated anger means 5.46 and 6.06 on a 1–7 scale, so its comparison is lower anger rather than an emotion-free baseline. Anger and frustration are averaged, limiting emotion specificity despite the theory distinguishing them. Scenarios also change delay, prior poor service and time spent; this is not an isolated incidental-anger manipulation.
study.study_3: All participants read the angry scenario. The design is three cue bundles × two outcomes, ambiguous versus resolved, not anthropomorphism × anger. Reported recruitment 419 minus 52 exclusions equals 367, whereas the text says 365 and main-model residual df 359 supports 365; an earlier manipulation-check df supports 367. No invented resolution of the two-person discrepancy.
study.study_3_results: The actual cue × outcome interaction is F(2,359) 2.64, p .07, not conventionally significant at .05. Under the ambiguous outcome, the three-group omnibus is significant and verbal-plus-visual differs from control, while verbal-only differs from neither. A significant linear trend is not a factorial demonstration of independent additive visual and verbal effects. Resolved-condition nulls do not prove equivalence or elimination.
study.study_4: 192 minus 21 exclusions leaves 171. Scenario × presentation is randomized. Pre-interaction efficacy expectations are measured first, then the simulated chat, then two purchase-intention items, then post-interaction efficacy. The formal purchase-intention interaction is F(1,167) 4.29, p .04. Angry-scenario means are 3.57 control versus 2.73 anthropomorphic; purchases and punitive motivation are not observed.
study.expectation_gap: Study 4 reports pre-expectations 4.94 control versus 5.50 anthropomorphic and post-efficacy 4.09 versus 3.88. Their pre-minus-post gaps are .85 versus 1.62. The presentation × time test is F(1,169) 7.31, p .01. A gap can change through either component, and the post rating follows the purchase outcome; the difference score is not a uniquely identified causal mediator.
study.mediation: Study 4’s PROCESS Model 15 uses 10,000 bootstrap samples. The moderated-mediation index is +.0279, CI [−.0778,.1562], containing zero. Conditional indirect effects are +.0675 [.0012,.1707] for anger and +.0396 [−.0408,.1468] for the comparison. The text names pre-interaction expectations as mediator, not unambiguously the pre-minus-post gap. Positive indirect effects must not be silently reversed to explain the negative overall response. Opposing paths can be valid, but coding and estimands are needed to interpret this claim.
study.study_5: 302 participants all read the angry scenario; two presentations × baseline/lowered-expectation introduction. Formal company-evaluation interaction F(1,298) 4.35, p .04. Baseline means are 4.63 control versus 3.90 anthropomorphic; with the disclaimer they are 4.25 versus 4.32, nonsignificant. This is conditional rating evidence, not equivalence, improved actual service, proven unique mediation or a validated production intervention.
study.pretest_limits: Nonsignificant gender or warmth midpoint tests are not equivalence tests. Study 5’s pretest means around five suggest a different scale anchor from earlier tests, but its anchors are not sufficiently specified here: do not declare the avatar non-neutral or silently assume the earlier midpoint.
study.application: Explain capabilities truthfully, test user expectations against demonstrated performance and provide effective recourse. The paper does not justify concealing capabilities, intentionally disappointing people, denying human help or deploying covert emotion profiling. Historical forecasts about humanlike AI by 2029 are cited speculation, not a current validated forecast.

summary: Strengthen existing anthropomorphism and expectation-disconfirmation records with context-sensitive service evidence, real interaction tests and explicit mediation limits. Keep agency and blame as theoretical boundaries rather than measured outcomes. No new synonym row is warranted.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the bounded service-interaction evidence to an existing construct; a negative expectation gap is not a separate synonym entry.

evidence.quote: the attribution of humanlike properties, characteristics, or

findings.evidence_scope: Name, avatar and first-person cue bundles change evaluations in some simulated service contexts. Several formal scenario interactions support conditional effects, while the field association is observational and Study 3’s cue × outcome interaction has p .07.
findings.boundary: Humanlike cues, perceived human likeness, actual capabilities and actual mental states differ. Do not generalize an angry service scenario into a universal penalty or infer sentience, actual customer retaliation or performance from a rating.

findings.definition: Appraising a result as falling short of or exceeding prior expectations by comparing expected and perceived performance.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the bounded service-interaction evidence to an existing construct; a negative expectation gap is not a separate synonym entry.

evidence.quote: mance fails to meet expectations, the negative disconﬁrmation

findings.evidence_scope: The paper uses expectancy violation for perceived performance falling below prior expectations. Studies 4–5 measure pre/post efficacy and manipulate an expectation-setting introduction. This is a negative-performance-gap refinement of the existing broader appraisal, not a separate row.
findings.boundary: A significant pre/post contrast and an expectation-message interaction do not identify a unique causal pathway. The moderated-mediation index includes zero, conditional indirect effects are positive, and post-efficacy follows purchase intention. Truthful calibration is different from strategic capability understatement.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the bounded service-interaction evidence to an existing construct; a negative expectation gap is not a separate synonym entry.

findings.evidence_scope: The conceptual framework proposes that humanlike cues raise expected agency, including ability to take action. The experiments measure anthropomorphism or expected efficacy rather than independently establishing the complete agency-to-blame chain.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only conceptual link. Capability expectations and agency attributions are related but distinct; these data do not demonstrate actual machine intentions, moral agency or legal accountability.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Add the bounded service-interaction evidence to an existing construct; a negative expectation gap is not a separate synonym entry.

evidence.quote: to blame others and retaliate when another’s performance falls

findings.evidence_scope: Blame and punitive responses motivate the theoretical account. Main experimental dependent variables are satisfaction, company evaluation and purchase intentions, not direct blame allocations, observed retaliation or validated punishment motives.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only theoretical interpretation. Low ratings or willingness not to purchase can be reasonable quality judgments; they do not alone demonstrate blame, unfair scapegoating or deliberate punitive intent.

public_supplement.reading: Complete extracted text read; supplementary images unavailable for visual inspection. No local PDF, checksum, raw data or code obtained.
public_supplement.findings: Alternative anger classifiers retain domain-shift concerns; supplementary agreement is not independent ground truth. Company-evaluation replication retains 179 participants and reports a formal interaction. The sadness experiment retains 192 and reports an opposite conditional pattern, but the pretest’s printed sadness means oppose its wording. Appendix M’s nonsignificant within-presentation comparisons do not establish improvement or equivalence; such contrasts are not inherently invalid. Study 5 figure labels agree with main cell means. Scripts label the resolved manipulation as Study 4, whereas the main design places it in Study 3.
public_supplement.limits: No additional ontology term, paper credit or production policy is inferred from these supplementary checks. Image-only details and exact mediator coding remain unverified.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The histogram visibly labels bars at 1, 3, 4 and 5 as 22,984, 10,979, 130 and 536, with no visible bar at 2. Those labeled counts total 34,629 rather than the reported 34,639 and do not reconcile with the stated rating mean 2.165 or SD .799. Ask for the correct distribution; do not reconstruct missing customer records or replace the authoritative summary from an ambiguous chart.

Reported anger mean .064 minus one SD 1.706 equals −1.642, outside the support of a nonnegative LIWC proportion. It cannot describe lower-but-present observed anger as written. Exact probing values, transformations and nonlinear marginal-effect estimands are not supplied; do not replace the printed marginal slopes with naive coefficient arithmetic.

419 recruited minus 52 exclusions equals 367, not the printed 365. Main ANOVA and t-test degrees of freedom fit 365, while an earlier manipulation check fits 367. No data or exclusion history obtained to resolve the two observations.

Text alternates between pre-interaction expectations and a calculated expectation gap and describes lowered expectations where the theory predicts inflated expectations. Positive conditional indirect effects and a null moderated-mediation index remain as printed; suppression is possible, but the exact estimated pathways cannot be recovered from narrative alone.

The reported gender/warmth means and t tests appear to use a midpoint near five rather than earlier midpoint four. Scale anchors were not obtained. A nonsignificant midpoint comparison is not equivalence regardless of the intended midpoint.

Primary publisher reports 27 August 2021; Crossref reports 3 November 2021. Preserve both with provenance and use 2022 for the issue citation; do not treat either filename or PDF metadata as decisive.

methodological_limits: A single-company selected-rating field sample and several MTurk simulations are not an effect estimate for all service customers or current generative systems. Sessions, text entries, participants and pretest participations must remain distinct.

Observed name use can reflect convention or repeated failed requests rather than validated agency perception. Recognition confidence is not independently verified understanding. The selection model relies on untested exclusion assumptions.

Scenario manipulations bundle emotion, delay, prior service quality and time costs. Lower-anger comparisons are not emotion-free baselines; averaging anger with frustration limits specific emotion attribution.

Preserve formal interaction evidence in Studies 2, 4 and 5 and the field robustness test. Study 3 has an outcome interaction with p .07; simple-effect significance differences do not upgrade that result. Nulls do not establish equivalence.

Expectations and ratings are not actual task performance, purchases, punitive motives or unique causal mediators. Post-outcome measurement and reported indirect-effect signs require careful interpretation.
Bundled verbal and visual cues do not isolate each feature. Linear trends do not demonstrate independent additivity. Avatar midpoint null tests do not establish psychological neutrality.

Accurate capability disclosure and meaningful human recourse should be evaluated directly. No consent, privacy, effectiveness or fairness validation is supplied for emotion-responsive deployment suggestions.
Public metadata verifies identity, not every cited claim. No unread original emotion theory, cited book, supplementary image or unexecuted code receives independent evidence credit.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Keep subjective helpfulness and customer evaluation separate from objective quality or clinical benefit. Post-outcome measurements cannot automatically establish an earlier causal mechanism.
Opposing indirect and direct paths can be valid. Retain printed signs and distinguish total effects from conditional mediation rather than silently repairing an inconvenient coefficient.
Preserve genuine formal interactions while correcting narrow reporting mistakes. Expectation is proposed rather than automatically measured by every responsibility or satisfaction outcome.
Attitude-dependent evaluation need not be irrational or punitive. A customer can reasonably lower a rating when service does not meet a legitimate need.

deferred.reason: Background theories discuss incidental anger, but these studies use service-related emotional scenarios or measured session language. No unrelated anger induction or complete primary theory reading establishes the proposed separate construct.
No direct motive or real purchasing/retaliation outcome is measured in the main experiments. Lower evaluation can be warranted dissatisfaction.
